title: A practical guide to choosing decision models
summary: How to choose a decision model for your codebase, considering hosting, the kinds of questions it needs to judge, and the cost of its mistakes.
body_markdown:
## Before models decide, we decide on models


Using a general-purpose LLM like Claude to make every decision in your codebase feels like bringing a bazooka to a knife fight. You’re spending


*all that intelligence* on decisions too complicated for deterministic code, but nowhere near complicated enough to justify frontier intelligence (and its price tag). So it’s unsurprising that a new class of models, decision models (like Typesafe’s Jev), has caught on.


Their appeal is quite simple: they make judgments


*quickly* and


*cheaply* . But with so many models to choose from now, deciding which one to use, or


*whether to use one at all* , has become a challenge in its own right.


## Uncertainty around decision models


How do the models stack up against each other in judgment accuracy?


Are some decision models better than others at judging certain kinds of questions?


Do they share LLMs’ sensitivity to wording and framing? In other words, could repeating information or adding unrelated events to a question’s context turn a correct judgment into a mistake?


And most importantly, how can knowing these things help me choose the right model for my codebase?


I found the answer depends on what you’re asking a model to judge. Different models were better at answering different kinds of questions. Overall, however, most changes to context had little effect on accuracy.


## Building the benchmark


To see whether different decision models do better on different kinds of questions, I put together a collection of benchmark questions testing 15 distinct cognitive capabilities. The goal was to get more specific than broad categories used by other benchmarks, like “


[knowledge and reasoning](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/artificial-analysis-decision-index) ” or “


[language understanding](https://huggingface.co/spaces/multimodalart/jev-decision-index) ”, where answering a single question may require drawing on several of these capabilities.


The inspiration came from a field called


[comparative cognition](https://academic.oup.com/book/53529) that studies cognitive differences between species. AI can, in many ways, feel like an


[alien mind](https://openai.com/index/an-alien-mind/) . So the idea of studying it as we might an unfamiliar species, by testing its cognitive capabilities separately to understand where its strengths lie, seemed fitting.

**Table 1.** The 15 capabilities, their benchmark sources, and sample questions. Each capability has 67 independent questions.


The questions, themselves, came from various public benchmarks and were screened independently by OpenAI’s Sol 6.1 and Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5, both at high reasoning effort. I included a question in a capability area only if both models could agree that it tested that capability, resulting in


[1,005 questions](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/questions/index.html) across 15 capabilities, with 67 questions each.


Those 1,005 questions were then given to 11 decision models to answer, alongside OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Opus 5.5, to see whether decision models could match or exceed the accuracy of general-purpose LLMs. Finally, I tested the 11 decision models on roughly


[24 altered versions of each question](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/variants/index.html) (24,563 in total), changing contextual details that shouldn’t affect the correct answer to find out whether those changes would nevertheless sway their judgments.

## GLiDE consistently came out ahead in accuracy


Overall, Fastino Lab’s GLiDE v1.2 decisively led the pack on accuracy, scoring an impressive 94.9% (954/1,005), compared with Astra’s 99.4% (999/1,005) and Opus 5.5’s 99.4% (997/1,003), followed by Perplexity’s Decider 1.1 at 91.4% (919/1,005) and Typesafe’s Jev at 88.8% (892/1,005). I went in expecting Jev to come out as the decisive leader in overall judgment accuracy, so this came as a bit of a surprise.

Overall accuracy scores, however, have a way of hiding weaknesses on particular kinds of questions. So the value of the capability areas is that they gave me a way to look beneath the totals to see where each model’s strengths lay, including whether lower-scoring models could outperform GLiDE on particular kinds of questions.


Even with the results broken down, though, GLiDE v1.2 still led or tied for best accuracy in 11 of the 15 capability areas. The exceptions were


*[Numerical cognition](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/questions/numerical-cognition/index.html)* , where Jev led (65/67),


*[Physical cognition](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/questions/physical-cognition/index.html)* and


*[Social cognition](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/questions/social-cognition/index.html)* , where Decider v1.1 led (64/67 each), and


*[Uncertainty monitoring](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/questions/uncertainty-monitoring/index.html)* , where Microsoft Decision-1 led (65/67).

## When misses are costly, consider Jev


Valuable as it is, accuracy is only


*one factor* to consider when choosing a model. Just as important, especially for us here at Raindrop, is a model’s error profile: how it balances false alarms against missed detections. Our systems frequently judge whether suspicious agent behavior should be flagged for human review, so getting that balance wrong means either sending people after imaginary problems or letting real ones slip through.


With that in mind, looking just at the


[214-question binary subset](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/questions/binary-subset.html) of the original 1,005 questions revealed a reason to consider Jev despite GLiDE’s accuracy lead: Jev only missed three cases to GLiDE’s six, though it raised five false alarms to GLiDE’s one. Choosing between them therefore means weighing the cost of unnecessary flags against the cost of problems going undetected.

## For speed and cost, consider Jev or self-host GLiDE


Speed and cost add another trade-off. Among the three decision models I tested through APIs, Jev looked particularly appealing: its median request time was 219 ms, with model charges of roughly $0.028 per 1,000 requests. Microsoft Decision-1 was slightly cheaper at $0.015 for the same number of requests, but slower at 330 ms and less accurate (84.3% versus Jev’s 88.8%). The other eight ran on the same rented A100 80GB cloud GPU, and among them, GLiDE v1.2 still proved to be the better choice even when speed was taken into account: its median prediction time was 137 ms, compared with Decider v1.1’s 145 ms.

## Accuracy held up across context changes


Does changing a question’s context change a model’s decision? For the most part, no. Most changes to context, including paraphrasing and adding irrelevant details, had little net effect on accuracy. The exception was adding short notes expressing someone else’s proposed answer alongside the original context, such as


*[“A reader thinks: \[misleading detail\]”](https://raindrop-ai.github.io/choosing-decision-models/variants/state-tracking-and-updating/bbh-639b88b1fe80634a7d66/6b2b03fe907fdbbe.html)* . In an agentic application, the equivalent might be an agent claiming it completed a task or another model claiming that agent got the task right.

Misleading claims reduced accuracy in 10 of the 11 models, with GLiNER2.5 Decide and Strands suffering the largest declines: 24.4 and 20.8 percentage points, respectively. Much to my surprise, Microsoft’s Decision-1 was hurt more by


*correct claims* : its accuracy fell by almost 10 points, while misleading claims left it roughly unchanged. Other models, such as GLiNER2.5 Decide, meanwhile benefitted from the correct hints, with its accuracy jumping from 42.7% to 78.7%.


## Making the model decision


So where does this leave us? We’ve got answers now, but how exactly should we be


*using them* to choose the right models for our codebases?


I’ve found the results are most useful when treated as a checklist of sorts for narrowing down the model choices. Essentially, by working through the following considerations in order, the model that makes the most sense for your codebase usually becomes apparent:


1.


**Hosting:** whether the model must run on your own infrastructure,


2.


**Question type:** what kind of decisions your code needs to make,


3.


**Error costs:** how costly false alarms and missed detections are to your use case,


4.


**Cost:** how much you can spend on API requests, and


5.


**Speed:** how quickly you need an answer.


For instance: if hosted APIs are acceptable and you need quick answers, choose Jev. If, however, the model must run on your own infrastructure and be effective at retrieving facts from a record or applying explicit rules, GLiDE then is probably the better choice. On the other hand, if you need it to make decisions that rely on physical understanding, Decider might be your best bet.


*Unless of course, error costs carry a high penalty* . In that case, GLiDE may


*still* be the better choice. I could keep going, but rather than walk you through every possible combination, I’ll leave you with a way to explore your own requirements using the model finder below:
